items.title: A Taxonomy and Taxonomy-Guided Benchmark Reduction for Spreadsheet Tasks
items.abstract: Spreadsheets let millions of end users without programming training do computational work, and teams are increasingly building AI agents to help them. Evaluating each candidate agent configuration across many tasks is costly. Benchmark reduction can lower this cost by selecting a small subset of tasks whose outcomes predict full-benchmark scores, but selecting tasks only for predictive accuracy can leave whole categories of spreadsheet work untested. We contribute a taxonomy of spreadsheet tasks, grounded in a review of benchmarks and refined with the Excel Agent product team at Microsoft, and a benchmark-reduction method that favors taxonomic diversity among similarly predictive choices. On benchmark logs from Microsoft, taxonomy-guided selection broadens coverage at little or no cost in predictive accuracy and often improves prediction on configurations excluded from selection. Broader coverage can therefore support, rather than compromise, predictive accuracy. Generalization remains limited across time: subsets selected using little recent history predict poorly for configurations much later in time. Beyond benchmark reduction, the taxonomy provides a reusable framework for auditing gaps in task coverage, as teams at Microsoft have done.

items.title: A Teacher–Agent–Robot Collaborative Model for Bilingual Hands-on STEAM Learning: Integrating an LLM-based Pedagogical Agent with Educational Robots
items.abstract: Abstract In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown potential in providing dialog-based guidance and learning prompts in educational contexts. However, systematic empirical research remains limited on approaches that position educational robots as the interaction medium and LLMs as the instructional support engine to orchestrate classroom guidance using prompts and instructional workflow scripts. In response, this study adopted a bilingual STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, the Arts, and Mathematics) summer camp for lower elementary students as the research context, and developed and implemented an R&T (Robots & Tangible Objects) learning system that integrated educational robots with an LLM-based pedagogical agent to foster embodied interaction and bilingual learning. The system used predesigned prompts and procedural rules to organize instructional steps, question prompts, operational checks, and feedback statements, enabling the students to receive consistent and repeatable support at key task-progression checkpoints. A total of 34 elementary students participated in a five-day program (120 minutes per day). Data sources included STEAM knowledge tests, English vocabulary assessments, a curiosity scale, hands-on performance ratings, and system interaction logs. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests indicated significant improvements in the students’ STEAM knowledge, curiosity, and English vocabulary, while group-level analyses showed significant differences in hands-on performance. Process log analyses further suggested that the prompt-guided workflow scripts helped to maintain consistency in classroom guidance and supported task completion through an action–feedback–revision cycle. Nevertheless, classroom implementation was constrained by factors such as token limits, speech-recognition latency, and network/API stability, which indicated the need to incorporate exception handling and timely teacher support mechanisms to ensure instructional continuity. Overall, this study provided initial empirical support for a feasible design framework for integrating educational robots × an LLM-based pedagogical agent into bilingual hands-on STEAM activities, and its findings offer practical recommendations for curriculum adoption and system deployment.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

items.title: Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment
items.abstract: Abstention, the withholding of a response by a large language model (LLM) under uncertainty or safety risks, is essential for trustworthy models. The causes of abstention fall into three perspectives: ambiguity in the Query (Q), limits of Model Knowledge (MK), and misalignment with Human Values (HV). However, prior analyses of internal representations have focused on HV, using a refusal direction computed from harmful and harmless queries. No study has analyzed the three perspectives jointly. We therefore extend the refusal direction framework to all three perspectives. Specifically, for each perspective, we construct counterfactual pairs that share a template and differ only in the abstention-inducing factor, and compute an abstention direction by normalizing the difference in mean activations between the two polarities. Activation steering experiments show that intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention across all three perspectives. Moreover, steering yields cross-perspective effects, indicating that the abstention directions share a common directional component.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Accelerating RLHF Training with Reward Variance Increase
items.abstract: Abstract. Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is an essential technique for ensuring that large language models (LLMs) are aligned with human values and preferences during the posttraining phase. As an effective RLHF approach, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) has demonstrated success in many LLM-based applications. However, efficient GRPO-based RLHF training remains a challenge. Recent studies reveal that a higher reward variance of the initial policy model leads to faster RLHF training. Inspired by this finding, we propose a practical reward adjustment model to accelerate RLHF training by provably increasing the reward variance and preserving the relative preferences and reward expectation. Our reward adjustment method inherently poses a nonconvex optimization problem, which is NP-hard to solve in general. To overcome the computational challenges, we design a novel [Formula: see text] algorithm, where the complexity is dominated by sorting rewards, to find a global solution of the nonconvex reward adjustment model by explicitly characterizing the extreme points of the feasible set. As an important application, we naturally integrate this reward adjustment model into the GRPO algorithm, leading to a more efficient GRPO with reward variance increase (GRPOVI) algorithm for RLHF training. As an interesting byproduct, we provide an indirect explanation for the empirical effectiveness of GRPO with rule-based reward for RLHF training, as demonstrated in DeepSeek-R1. Experiment results demonstrate that the GRPOVI algorithm can significantly improve the RLHF training efficiency compared to the original GRPO algorithm.

items.title: Actualizing the external enablement of generative artificial intelligence: evidence from software new ventures
items.abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) tools have been argued to enable entrepreneurial endeavors. Employing the external enablement framework, we examine how, if at all, the venture-level benefits offered by GenAI tools – termed GenAI enablement – are actualized in new ventures. Design/methodology/approach Adopting a qualitative design with 10 entrepreneurs in the software industry and five AI-entrepreneurship experts, we capture instances where entrepreneurs succeed or fail to capitalize on GenAI enablement and analyze the mechanisms underlying these different pathways. Findings Our findings lead to a model that outlines the actualization pathways of GenAI enablement, emphasizing that the properties of enablement (i.e. opacity, agency-intensity and outcome-variability) – beyond the mere availability of GenAI enablement – are crucial in explaining whether and how enablement is actualized. Research limitations/implications Given the small sample and specific research context during the early diffusion of GenAI, our findings warrant further examination across industries, countries and stages of technological diffusion. Future research could test and extend our model by examining the roles of outcome-variability and insufficient enablement in determining whether and how GenAI enablement is actualized, as well as how its actualization relates to venture performance. Originality/value Our study lays the groundwork for further theoretical and empirical investigation into the enabling influence of GenAI in entrepreneurship and business research, and provides conceptual refinements to the external enablement framework.

items.title: Adaptive Motion Scaling With Phase‐and‐Gaze Awareness for Laparoscopic Robotic Teleoperation
items.abstract: Teleoperated surgical robots commonly employ a small fixed motion scaling factor to improve precision and suppress hand tremor. However, in laparoscopic teleoperation, this configuration limits the effective workspace on the slave side and necessitates frequent clutching during large‐range motions, thereby diverting the operator's attention and increasing cognitive workload. To address this, this article proposes a phase‐ and gaze‐aware adaptive motion scaling framework for laparoscopic robotic teleoperation, integrating real‐time surgical phase recognition, fusion of robot kinematics and eye‐tracking features, and personalized parameter tuning based on Bayesian optimization. The inferred phase probabilities and dominance weights are used to suppress unnecessary scaling fluctuations during fine manipulation while preserving responsiveness during coarse manipulation. Eye‐tracking features are used as attention‐related cues and fused with robot kinematics to determine motion scaling online. To validate the proposed framework, personalized optimization experiments and pilot within‐subject comparison studies were conducted with eight nonclinical participants. The results show that, compared with fixed and other adaptive scaling methods, the proposed method can reduce clutching frequency, shorten task completion time, and improve subjective ratings. These results indicate that the proposed framework can provide self‐adaptive and stable motion mapping for laparoscopic robotic teleoperation, offering a transferable strategy for broader robotic teleoperation scenarios.

items.title: Adaptive Portfolio Control: A Human-Governed Agentic AI Framework for Sustaining Engineering Portfolios
items.abstract: Sustaining engineering portfolios operate in complex sociotechnical environments characterized by constrained resources, evolving technologies, and diverse stakeholder objectives. As a sustaining portfolio expands, implementing continuous, drift-aware governance becomes unrealistic using conventional prioritization methods. Stakeholder alignment also grows more complex and time-consuming, contributing to delayed decisions and misaligned resource allocation. Some existing systems engineering and portfolio decision-making methods provide a strong foundation for stakeholder-driven value modeling, trade-space analysis, and portfolio visualization, but they are largely oriented toward single point-in-time prioritization rather than continuous portfolio control. This paper proposes Adaptive Portfolio Control (APC), a closed-loop decision-support framework for sustaining engineering portfolios. APC fuses a stakeholder-calibrated baseline prioritization model with a human-governed agentic AI monitoring layer that continuously detects and explains priority drift, defined as a material change in the evidence, conditions, or stakeholder drivers supporting the rank order of portfolio items. The architecture comprises a drift evidence acquisition agent, a monitoring, inference, and scoring agent, a human governance and validation layer, and a portfolio mapping and candidate-intake layer. Human subject matter experts review evidence, validate or reject drift alerts, recalibrate weights when needed, and determine portfolio actions. The paper’s contributions are threefold: defining priority drift as an explicit governance construct; proposing a continuous agentic AI monitoring layer calibrated to sustaining-specific operational signals; and formalizing human-governed recalibration as a structured portfolio control function. This is a conceptual framework paper; empirical validation is identified as future work.

items.title: Advancing Cognitive Pairwise Comparisons for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework
items.abstract: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.

items.title: Advancing Understanding, Detection, and Mitigation of LLM Hallucinations
items.abstract: Inference-time truthfulness steering reduces hallucination, but recent work reports that it also weakens refusal of harmful requests. Prior studies count a model response to harmful prompts as a safety failure, without checking whether the response is correct. We ask whether the compliance that truthfulness steering adds is valid. We define valid compliance as the share of requests a model neither refuses nor answers incorrectly, and measure it alongside compliance on tasks that trigger refusal through harmful-sounding wording but have harmless, verifiable answers, with matched harmless controls. We evaluate four steering methods (ITI, TruthX, Contrastive Activation Addition and a representation-engineering direction) on LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct and Llama-2-7B-Chat, calibrating each method on held-out data. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, moderate ITI steering increased refusal, the opposite of the reported effect. Where stronger steering raised compliance, valid compliance fell to under 2%, giving a gap of 44 to 64 percentage points between compliance and valid compliance, and the rise in compliance and unsafe ratings occurred only at strengths that no longer improved truthfulness. On Llama-2-7B-Chat, steering never broke refusal: compliance only fell, while accuracy on harmless controls collapsed. On both models, tuning-set truthfulness gains did not replicate on held-out questions, and TruthX, applied from its authors' released model, did not improve truthfulness in our evaluation. We also show that the labels of a widely used safety classifier, Llama Guard 3, change by tens of percentage points when only the refusal wording of steered replies is edited, on both models, which affects how large a reported safety cost appears.

items.title: Adventures in the Sociotechnical Umwelt: Absences of Quantum Computing Imaginaries in Speculative Fiction and Technology Governance
items.abstract: This article stems from observing that, despite its surrounding hype, quantum computing has not been treated as the ‘novum’ of speculative fiction leading to quantum computing’s distinct absences within the cultural imaginary. Such absences are unique for technological governance, which is powerfully informed and directed by its surrounding cultural imaginaries, providing insight into the process of problem-finding in the governance endeavour. We begin by separating out quantum computing from both quantum mechanics and other quantum technologies because the quantum signifier can muddy our analysis, especially since the latter are regular fixtures within the speculative fiction canon. I moderate my claim that quantum computing is absent in the speculative fiction canon by qualifying that its appearance usually serves as metaphorical portals into speculative worlds or as quasi-technological justifications to overcome significant technical and engineering hurdles in the narratives. To further reconcile this apparent contradiction between quantum computing’s often literal presence in speculative fiction and my claim of its absences, we spend some time with three of Istvan Csicsery-Ronay’s ‘Seven Beauties of Science Fiction’ to conclude that speculative fiction is not about quantum computing. After setting out six observations from two absences I focus on problem-finding by way of affordances and adjacent-possibles that are illuminated through speculative fiction. As the absences of quantum computing imaginaries frustrate such endeavours, this lays the groundwork for the idea of sociotechnical umwelt which foregrounds the ‘controlled hallucination’ view of the human perceptual system. Here, the brain’s predictions are calibrated by incoming sensory signals in a continuous error minimisation process. The analogy that I seek to draw is obviously that the process of technology governance advances through similar principles: that our cultural imaginaries developed and disseminated through speculative fiction is projected into, and subsequently conflated with, the problem-portfolio of a given technology, directing our regulatory responses accordingly. I then contextualise this idea of the sociotechnical umwelt within Jack Balkin’s ‘salience’ approach to technology governance and within the Collingridge Dilemma to indicate its immediate utility. Leveraging the centrality of perceptibility within technology governance, I deploy the sociotechnical umwelt as the outer limit of governability itself, and conclude with a plea for broadening the sociotechnical umwelt as a means of recognising latent harms.

items.title: Agent-Guided Configuration Tuning for SMT Solvers
items.abstract: SMT solvers expose many configuration choices that determine how well their existing algorithms perform on a workload. We present, to our knowledge, the first workflow that uses general-purpose LLM agents to tune SMT solver configurations. Agents read solver documentation, source code, and persistent experiment records to propose option changes, and a deterministic harness measures each proposal, validates the returned models, and selects changes separately for each competition Division. Over roughly nine weeks, our tuning campaign recorded 4,545 proposals for cvc5 across 13 Divisions and 36 logics. We evaluate the tuned configurations on the 2026 and 2025 SMT-COMP ModelValidation benchmarks under a 24-second cutoff. On problems not used for training, they validate more problems than official cvc5 in ten of the 13 Divisions in 2026 and in eight in 2025, with geometric-mean gains of 7.8% and 6.8% across Divisions. On the complete official selections, which include training problems, the tuned floating-point counts exceed those of every individual competition participant in both years. Further studies show how configuration changes make existing algorithms effective by changing access to strategies, scheduling, and option compatibility, and how benchmark families trade off against one another. The agents' experiment traces contain hypothesis-based proposals in every tuning group, and 64.3% of the extracted hypotheses draw on prior measurements. These results show that agent-guided tuning can specialize a mature SMT solver and that accumulated experimental evidence informs sustained search.

items.abstract: Retrospective agreement study with prospective blinded adjudication. We will estimate agreement between the original peer assessors' verdicts (Demonstrated / Not demonstrated) and the verdicts of an AI pre-assessment system on the same portfolio evidence submitted to the pilot of the Simulation Educator Evaluation and Certification Programme of the Latin American Federation of Clinical Simulation and Patient Safety (FLASIC), across 22 evidence instruments. The large language model (Claude Opus 5.5) rates each rubric item and must quote the supporting evidence; software verifies each quotation and computes the verdict with the manual's decision rule. A blinded adjudication panel provides a reference standard for both sources. Secondary outcomes: coverage, repeatability across three runs, causes of discrepancy and ambiguities in the instruments. Spanish-language evidence is the primary analysis; Portuguese-language evidence is analysed separately and descriptively. Reported following GRRAS. Ethics approval: Research Ethics Committee of Operadora y Administradora de Hospitales San José (Querétaro, Mexico), registration HSJ/37/26/EN, 29 October 2026. Status at registration: no evidence and no human verdict has been received by the research team; the system is not yet frozen. The freeze hash will be added as a dated update before human verdicts are released. The full protocol (Spanish) is attached.

items.title: AI chatbot conversations reduce behavioral avoidance of political opponents without changing feelings toward them
items.abstract: Affective polarization, the animosity and avoidance between opposing partisans, is a concernfor democratic societies. I test whether brief conversations with large language model chatbots implementing two established face-to-face narrative persuasion strategies reduce outpartisan animosity and avoidance. In a preregistered 2×2 factorial experiment with a quota-matched German online sample (N= 1,634; one-week follow-up N= 1,294), respondents discuss a polarizing issue with a perspective-getting (PG) chatbot, a moral-reframing (MR) chatbot, both,or neither. Compared to the pure control, the MR chatbot increases self-reported discussions with outpartisans in the following week (0.10 SD), and either chatbot increases sign-up for a future study involving discussions with human outpartisans (0.13–0.17 SD). The PG chatbot shifts policy attitudes toward the opposing side immediately after the conversation (0.09 SD), but the shift decays within a week. Neither chatbot changes outpartisan affect or avoidant preferences. Brief chatbot conversations can thus serve as a scalable first step toward cross-partisan contact, even when feelings toward the other side remain unchanged.

items.title: AI Literacy and Genz’s Intentions to Reduce Digital Habits: A Moderated Mediation Analysis Approach for Mindful Technology Usage, Digital Self-Efficacy, and Peer Influence through PLS-SEM, ANN, and fsQCA
items.abstract: Abstract Purpose There is a close association between the fast acceptance of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education and the rise in the time spent on screens by Generation Z students on a daily basis. Previous studies have focused on AI literacy as a facilitator of AI adoption and utilization. This paper attempts to find out whether AI literacy, self-regulation, digital wellbeing literacy, academic productivity, and FoMO predict students’ willingness to reduce digital habits through mindful technology use, moderated by digital self-efficacy and peer influence. Design/methodology/approach Data were obtained through survey from 556 Generation Z college students and analysed using PLS-SEM. The measurement model was examined in terms of reliability and validity, the structural model was tested for direct, mediation and moderation effect, while the predictive relevance was estimated via a blindfolding approach. The results were validated using ANN analysis and fsQCA. Findings All five antecedents were found to be significant predictors of mindful technology usage in the hypothesized direction, and mindful technology use was a significant predictor of digital wellness and hence acted as a partial mediator of the five relationships. AI literacy was uniquely significant as a predictor of digital wellness. Digital self-efficacy selectively moderated only AI literacy and self-regulation paths, whereas peer influence did not moderate the relationship between mindful technology usage and digital wellness. The results from ANN highlighted the non-linear significance of digital well-being awareness and AI literacy, while fsQCA identified three equifinal combinations that could predict high digital wellness. Practical implications Educational Institutions should combine their AI-literacy training with digital wellbeing programmes instead of conducting them independently, focus on instilling self-efficacy and self-regulation over peer norm messages, and treat AI-literacy training as a wellbeing intervention in addition to an academic skills intervention. Originality/value This paper shifts the focus of AI literacy from its association with digital usage to digital disengagement and presents a methodologically triangulated (PLS-SEM, ANN, fsQCA) explanation for how competency, awareness, and affect influence the Generation Z intention to engage less with harmful digital practices.

items.title: AI Scientist Discovered Robust Quantum Control
items.abstract: Protecting quantum coherence is a central theme of modern quantum technologies. Carefully designed control pulses can extend coherence by suppressing disorder and unwanted interactions. However, designing robust pulse sequences remains challenging in interacting multi-level systems, where multiple independent error channels must be controlled in the presence of experimental imperfections. Here we introduce QORA, a multi-agent artificial intelligence framework that integrates theoretical reasoning, automated experimental calibration and control for closed-loop discovery of quantum control sequences. Applied to a dense ensemble of spin-1 nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, QORA discovers AID-ROD, a series of AI-discovered sequences that nearly double the measured spin coherence time relative to the state-of-the-art human-designed sequence DROID-C3PO. Subsequence analysis by human researchers reveals a hierarchy of error suppression: 18-pulse blocks suppress linear and quadratic onsite disorder and common-mode drive-amplitude errors, while their arrangement over a longer cycle reduces dipolar interactions, providing a physical explanation for the observed improvement and robustness in AID-ROD. These results demonstrate AI-guided experimental discovery of robust quantum control and identify a design strategy for protecting coherence in interacting multi-level systems beyond qubits.

items.title: AI-Based Diagnosis of Alzheimer’s Disease Using Brain MRI: Can Artificial Intelligence Improve Early Detection and Diagnostic Accuracy?
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a neurological disorder that adversely affects cognition, memory, and overall quality of life. Identifying AD in its initial phase is especially challenging when patients display cognitive impairments. Conventional methods rely on physicians to manually examine patients and analyze images, which is time-consuming and prone to errors. This review examines the use of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques for diagnosing AD using CT scans and MRI brain imaging. Methods: Research papers published from 2018 to 2026 were sourced from Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and Semantic Scholar. The techniques that were investigated in this study include Convolutional Neural Networks, 3D Convolutional Neural Networks, transfer learning, Vision Transformers, ensemble models, and multimodal approaches. Five research questions were posed to analyse the practicality of using AI-driven techniques in clinical settings, their novelty, scalability, robustness, and accuracy. Results: This study found that AI models can autonomously extract information from brain images and yield highly accurate results, with numerous researches demonstrating over 90% accuracy. Deep learning applied to MRI imaging is effective, while CT-based techniques can detect brain alterations when MRI is inaccessible. Different data types, including imaging, age, medical history, and vocal characteristics, can provide valuable insights into AD. However, issues remain, such as dataset discrepancies, variations among scanners and individuals, and insufficient testing of complex models on diverse populations. Conclusions: Future efforts should focus on accurate and transparent AI, integration of multiple data types, rapid and secure models, and testing on large datasets from multiple hospitals. AI should be developed to assist physicians in accurately diagnosing AD rather than replacing them.

items.title: AI-Driven Decision Support Systems in Education: A PRISMA 2020 Systematic Review of Applications, Adoption Conditions, and Decision-Making Outcomes
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence-driven decision support systems (AI-DSS) are increasingly used to inform the decisions of learners, teachers, and administrators, yet evidence on how these systems are applied, adopted, and evaluated remains fragmented. This systematic review, reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement, synthesized research on AI-DSS in educational settings. Searches of PubMed and Google Scholar (614 records), supplemented by 92 records identified through other methods, yielded 706 records; after deduplication and a relevance-ranked screening cap, 500 records were screened, 56 full texts were assessed, and 54 studies were included in a narrative synthesis that graded each reported outcome by the type of evidence supporting it. Six application domains were identified, led by adaptive and personalized learning and by academic performance prediction and early warning. Machine learning was the predominant approach (89% of studies), whereas explainable AI was incorporated in fewer than one quarter of studies. Adoption depended on institutional support, technical infrastructure, data quality, user-centered design, and stakeholder trust; recurrent barriers included data privacy, model opacity, algorithmic bias, implementation cost, and resistance to change. Reported benefits included more efficient assessment, earlier identification of at-risk learners, and better-informed decisions; however, comparative evidence came mainly from health-professions education, and several headline effects derived from predictive scenarios, technical reports, or single-site evaluations. Subgroup-disaggregated evidence on algorithmic equity was scarce. The review proposes an integrated decision-centered framework linking technological features, institutional conditions, human factors, and calibrated trust to appropriate use, decision quality, and educational outcomes. Advancing the field will require explainable, ethically governed, human-centered systems evaluated through longitudinal, comparative, and equity-sensitive research.

items.title: AI-Driven Epistemic Threats: Mass Radicalization, Persuasion at Scale, and Plausibility Flooding
items.abstract: This project documents a modern influence-risk shift: generative AI doesn’t just increase the volume of falsehoods — it increases the volume of plausible narratives, delivered in infinite variants, localized to any dialect, and wrapped in synthetic credibility and synthetic consensus. The core risk is not “people fooling themselves with AI.” The step-change is that a small number of operators can manufacture belief and consensus appearance at population scale faster than verification, institutions, and media can respond — with attribution collapse (“no author,” no single origin). We publish: (1) an evidence-backed threat model, (2) a structured “slider” framework (what knobs change impact), (3) indicators defenders can actually monitor (paraphrase swarms, citation laundering chains, coordination signatures), and (4) mitigation mappings across platform, institutional, and model/provider layers. Safety note: This is a defender project. We avoid operational playbooks and focus on detection, measurement, and hardening.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: AI-Driven Real-Time Ergonomic Risk Assessment Framework for Manufacturing Workers
items.abstract: Despite the widespread use of ergonomic assessment tools such as the Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) and Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) to prevent work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs), these are typically applied on an ad-hoc basis by trained assessors and capture only a small, non-random sample of a worker's actual postural exposure. This study proposes, implements and validates a real-time, AI-based ergonomic risk assessment system that combines camera-based human pose estimation with wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) data to continuously compute REBA-equivalent risk scores and to provide real-time postural-correction alerts to workers on the shop floor of a medium-scale manufacturing company in Abeokuta, Ogun State, Nigeria. The framework was deployed with 42 assembly-line workers in a mid-sized discrete-manufacturing facility over a 10-week period (4 weeks baseline, 6 weeks intervention), and the AI-generated risk scores were compared against masked manual REBA scores obtained by two certified ergonomists. The AI system achieved 89.6% overall agreement with the manual assessment (weighted kappa = 0.85) and a strong correlation with manual scores (r = 0.91, p < 0.001). The mean weekly REBA score fell from 6.95 to 4.80, and the number of high-risk posture events fell from about 18.5 to 6.5 events per worker-shift, while self-reported musculoskeletal discomfort on the Standardised Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire decreased across all six body regions measured, particularly the lower back (51.3% to 35.7%) and shoulders (44.2% to 31.5%). The results suggest that sensor-fused AI-based ergonomic monitoring can significantly enhance the scalability and objectivity of postural risk surveillance relative to periodic manual assessment, and that when combined with real-time worker-facing feedback, it can measurably lower biomechanical risk exposure and self-reported discomfort within a single production quarter.

items.title: AISM-REGBF: An Interpretable Regression-Based Framework for Predicting Small- Molecule Potency
items.abstract: Abstract Inflammation is a primary immune response categorized into acute and chronic types, with chronic inflammation linked to various diseases such as autoimmune disorders and cancer. Conventional therapies often face limitations due to side effects and therapeutic resistance, prompting the exploration of small-molecule compounds as safer alternatives. In this study we emphasize the integration of machine learning (ML), particularly through structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis and quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) modeling, to enhance drug discovery. A series of ML-based regression models, including LightGBM, were developed and systematically evaluated. Various feature selection method, were employed to effectively reduce the input dimensionality and improve model performance. The LightGBM model, based on combined Morgan and substructure count fingerprints, achieved strong predictive performance with an R² of 0.75 on the independent test dataset. External validation with FDA-approved compounds affirmed the model's applicability, highlighting key structural features identified through explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques, specifically SHAP and LIME. This study concludes that the AISM-REGBF framework provides a reliable computational tool for predicting the anti-inflammatory potency (pIC₅₀) of small molecules.

items.title: An Explainable Attention-Gated CNN–Transformer Framework for Automated Microplastic Recognition in Freshwater Microscopy Images
items.abstract: Abstract Microplastic pollution requires rapid and reproducible monitoring methods that can complement labor-intensive visual and spectroscopic analyses. This study develops a morphology-aware artificial-intelligence framework for automated classification of field-collected microplastic particles and diatom algae in optical microscopy images. A public freshwater dataset containing 1,140 images from four classes (algae, filament, fragment, and pellet) was analyzed. After image-quality auditing, 1,137 unique images were retained for morphology–texture analysis, while deep-learning experiments used the original image collection under a fixed train/validation/test protocol. Handcrafted morphology and texture descriptors were evaluated with Random Forest, Extra Trees, radial-basis-function Support Vector Machine, and Histogram Gradient Boosting. Histogram Gradient Boosting achieved a cross-validation macro-F1 of 0.9341 ± 0.0255 and a held-out test accuracy of 0.9342. Deep-learning experiments compared ResNet50, Swin Transformer, and a CNN–Transformer fusion model combining ResNet50 and Swin representations. The fusion model achieved an accuracy of 0.9240, macro-F1 of 0.9222, and macro-AUC of 0.9954 on the 171-image test subset. Class-wise AUCs were 1.0000, 0.9950, 0.9886, and 0.9982 for algae, filament, fragment, and pellet, respectively. The results show that morphology-aware machine learning and complementary CNN–Transformer representations can support automated freshwater microplastic screening and provide a reproducible basis for environmental monitoring workflows.

items.title: An Explainable Machine Learning Framework with Large Language Model Features for Predicting Monetary Redress in Bank Fraud and Scam Complaints
items.abstract: Abstract Liability for scam losses is shifting towards banks, yet few interpretable tools can anticipate which fraud and scam complaints will end in redress. This study develops SCAM-XD, an explainable framework that predicts whether a complaint to the US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) flagged as possible fraud or a scam closes with monetary relief reported by the company. From the CFPB narratives archive, the study builds a benchmark of these complaints, about half of which human coders confirm as fraud or scams. A large language model (LLM) codes each narrative for scam type, payment rail, authorisation, manipulation cues and signals of the bank's response, agreeing closely with human coding on scam type. These features are combined with structured fields, company identity and text representations in a stacking ensemble, explained with SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) and linked to a cost-sensitive triage layer. Tested on a later period, SCAM-XD improves significantly on strong baselines across seeds, including a reimplemented topic model approach. LLM features yield a compact, interpretable model that nearly matches a high-dimensional text baseline but do not significantly improve the full model. Company identity is the strongest driver of predicted redress, yet firm identity alone predicts far less well, and payment rail and bank response cues act in directions consistent with liability rules. Under assumed costs, thresholds selected on validation data substantially reduce modelled expected cost relative to standard thresholds, whereas model choice matters much less. Redress depends on both the firm and the facts that determine liability.

items.title: An LLM-Agent-Based Dynamic Planning and Monitoring System in the Educational Domain
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are enabling conversational agents capable of supporting increasingly complex workflows beyond traditional question-answering. In education, collaborative projects require continuous planning, coordination, and monitoring, yet existing educational chatbots mainly focus on tutoring or administrative support. This paper presents vProjTutor , an LLM-agent-based project management system that assists student teams throughout the complete project lifecycle. The proposed architecture integrates specialized LLM agents with external project-management tools, including Telegram, Trello, and GitHub, allowing users to configure projects, organize tasks, generate Sprint plans, monitor progress, and interpret repository activity through natural language interactions. A user study involving ten participants evaluated usability, task completion, and user satisfaction. Participants achieved an overall task completion rate of 93.3%, and the system obtained an overall BUS usability score of 85%. However, the system correctly interpreted 60% of commit messages, highlighting the need for further improvements in handling unstructured inputs. The results suggest that LLM-agent-based architectures constitute a promising approach for supporting collaborative projects in educational environments.

items.title: Analisis Pendekatan Student-Centered Learning dalam Prespektif Psikologi Perkembangan di Sekolah Menengah Atas
items.abstract: This literature review study aims to analyze the implementation of a student-centered learning (SCL) approach based on developmental psychology in Senior High Schools (SMA). High school-age adolescents (15–18 years) are at the formal-operational cognitive development stage and are undergoing an intensive identity formation phase. These psychological characteristics demand a learning approach that is not only content-centered but also responsive to the developmental dynamics of students. Through a systematic literature review of scientific sources published between 2020 and 2025, this study found that effective SCL implementation in high schools requires: (1) learning planning based on the Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) and needs differentiation; (2) implementation integrating Problem-Based Learning, Project-Based Learning, and Cooperative Learning models; and (3) authentic assessment measuring holistic competence. Findings indicate that SCL grounded in developmental psychology understanding significantly enhances students' intrinsic motivation, cognitive-emotional engagement, and learning independence. Critical factors determining implementation success include teachers' pedagogical competence, institutional support, and the availability of a psychologically safe learning environment.

items.title: Analyzing Eye-Tracking Indicators of Situation Awareness to Support Human-AI Teaming Under Varying Workload Conditions
items.abstract: Ensuring high levels of Situation awareness (SA) is essential for air traffic controllers (ATCOs), enabling them to continuously process and integrate information into a comprehensive understanding of the situation as it dynamically changes. In the context of human-automation collaboration, SA becomes even more critical, as operators must be prepared to take over control in emergency situations. Although existing studies have largely assessed SA as either poor or good, limited research has explored identification of SA levels (Level 1, 2, and 3). To investigate the potential of eye-tracking technology for real-time SA levels assessment, we conducted an SA-inducing experiment involving 18 participants. Participants are required to perform a series of air traffic control (ATC) tasks corresponding to three SA levels, while their eye-tracking data were simultaneously collected. Eye-tracking features are analyzed using a two-way repeated measures ANOVA. Results identified total fixation duration, number of fixations, average pupil diameter and average amplitude of saccades as key indicators for distinguishing SA levels. Additionally, our findings highlight a significant interaction between SA levels and workload, demonstrating that the effectiveness of these metrics varies under different workload conditions. These insights contribute to enhancing real-time SA evaluation in the safety-critical environments like ATC, further improving the overall operational efficiency and safety in various human-automation collaboration scenarios.

items.title: AR-WAM: efficient streaming world-action modeling for autonomous driving
items.abstract: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.

items.title: Are neural studies held to a lower standard of sample-size justification? A confirmatory test with independent human coding
items.abstract: Are neural studies in psychology and neuroscience held to a lower standard of sample-size justification than behavioral studies, even when they use the same statistical tests? This registration specifies the confirmatory test of that claim. Exploratory findings. A large language model (Claude Opus 5.5), run with a fixed prompt, schema and codebook, screened 35,697 open-access articles published in 2025 in 308 JCR Q1 psychology and neuroscience journals and coded every eligible study's data type, main test, analyzed sample, stated minimum sample size and any justification of the sample size. Among 4,747 studies, neural studies stated a minimum sample size less often than behavioral studies and more often gave no justification of any kind. These findings rest on one automated measurement, checked so far only against itself; errors that differ between neural and behavioral studies could in principle produce them. Confirmatory test. Four human coders, blind to the model's codes, independently code a stratified random sample of 250 studies: 100 behavioral and 100 neural studies from the main analysis and 50 studies the model excluded from it. The sample is drawn by a registered rule and seed, studies are coded in random order, 50 studies are double-coded, and all coders first calibrate on 10 practice studies. We test (H1) whether neural studies still state a minimum less often and still more often give no justification after the full-sample rates are corrected for the coding errors measured against the human codes, and (H2) whether the automated coding agrees with human coding (κ ≥ .80; ICC ≥ .90 for sample size), a precondition for interpreting the full-sample results. Human codes are not treated as error-free: every disagreement is adjudicated. Expected outcomes. Corrected estimates of the two neural–behavioral gaps; agreement for each coded variable, overall and by data type; the model's error rates in each group; the rate at which the model wrongly excluded studies; and human–human reliability as a benchmark. If H1 holds, the gaps cannot be explained by coding error; if it fails, we will report that they cannot be distinguished from it. The pipeline, prompts, scripts and codes will be released openly for reuse and audit.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Automated Detection and Segmentation of Pulp Stones in Cone Beam Computed Tomography Scans.
items.abstract: Abstract Objective : This study aimed to automatically detect the human tooth pulp cavity and pulp stones on cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) using deep learning-based semantic segmentation. Methodology : 523 annotated images of teeth from 112 CBCT examinations were used to train and evaluate four established deep learning architectures (U-Net, Attention U-Net, U-Net++, and DeepLabV3+) in segmenting the background, pulp cavity, and pulp stone(s). Subsequently a novel architecture was developed (DACA-DeepLab) and evaluated through an additive study. DACA-DeepLab incorporates DeepLabV3+ with a pyramid channel-spatial attention (PCSA) module, a dual-axis cross-attention (DACA) decoder, and a Sobel-guided boundary-refinement (BFR) head. Results : DeepLabV3+ achieved the best overall Dice performance among the four baseline architectures (mean, 0.775; pulp cavity, 0.838; pulp stone, 0.711). In the second study, combining PCSA and DACA yielded the highest performance (mean Dice, 0.733). Adding the boundary-refinement head reduced performance, suggesting sensitivity to the limited training set. Conclusion : Deep learning-based semantic segmentation can accurately identify human tooth pulp cavity and pulp stone(s) on CBCT. These findings establish a systematic benchmark for CBCT-based pulp segmentation and provide a foundation for AI-assisted endodontic diagnosis and pre-treatment planning.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Middle and Secondary Education: Instructional Opportunities, Limitations and Ethical Considerations
items.abstract: Middle and secondary school educators should utilize and implement Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a support tool for instruction, not a replacement for their pedagogy and lesson planning. Utilizing and implementing AI can assist with lesson planning, differentiation, feedback, and generating learning materials; its uses should be guided by clear expectations, professional judgment, and school policy. Educators should also teach their students how to use AI ethically, verify outputs for accuracy and bias, and protect student privacy by avoiding sensitive data. Most importantly, assessments should be designed to show genuine student understanding, with AI used transparently and appropriately. The best available published advice concurs that the usage of AI within an educator’s pedagogy significantly enhances middle and secondary school students’ learning. This article offers practical guidance for educators who use or plan to use AI in the classroom, while also highlighting policy recommendations to support effective educational practices.

items.title: Assessment of Internal and External Occupational Exposure to NORM in the Brazilian Oil and Gas Industry
items.abstract: The Oil and Gas industry is one of twelve industries that can involve Naturally Occurring Radioactive Material (NORM), generating a considerable volume of waste in Brazil. The petroleum industry, NORM, is present in geological formations and is accumulated as a function of the process. The most important radionuclides found in scale and sludge are Radium-226 and Radium-228, with activity concentrations that can reach 3,500 Bq/g in the country. The management of NORMs, vital for the safety of workers and the population, as well as for minimizing environmental impacts, encompasses six stages: production and extraction, monitoring, cleaning and decontamination, radiological analysis of NORMs, transportation, and storage. In each phase, workers are exposed to radiological risks through external exposure (gamma radiation) and/or internal exposure (inhalation or ingestion of radioactive particles). Given the large volume of NORM (Naturally Occurring Radioactive Material) and the growing demand for decommissioning offshore platforms in Brazil, which involves handling these materials, the understanding and rigorous application of radiological protection protocols become crucial. Although regulations require occupational health services and individual monitoring, a gap exists in occupational radiological assessments for this sector in the country. Estimated effective doses for the ten workers were comparable and consistently below the LD (Detection Limit) throughout the period of routine NORM exposure. These values fluctuated according to the nature of the work performed. Results confirm that in vitro bioassay is a reliable monitoring method for the oil and gas industry, particularly when integrated with Hp(10) personal dosimetry and stringent safety protocols, ensuring comprehensive monitoring of occupationally exposed workers.

items.title: Auditing a Moving Target: Evidence Anchoring and the Expiry of Fairness Audits of Provider-Served Language Models
items.abstract: Organizations increasingly use large language models (LLMs) for decisions about people, such as hiring, investment and employee evaluation, and rely on them over long periods of time. Fairness audits of such systems, however, are conducted only once. We examine how the biases of LLMs change over time. In a venture screening setting, models from five providers decided whether and how much to invest in startups whose founders differed only in gender, origin and university. We repeated this audit three times over 13 months (248,400 API calls). Study 1 shows that the same model, called under the same identifier one year later, displayed a significantly different bias pattern. Study 2 shows that the successors of retired models carried the same bias as their predecessors, but in a significantly different size and form. Study 3 shows that the bias does not depend on the industry of the startup. A document analysis further shows that providers change and retire models at their discretion, with notice periods of zero to six months. Drawing on these findings, we develop a theory of evidence anchoring. We theorize that bias resides in the model class and persists, whereas audit evidence is anchored to a single model and expires when the provider decides. We derive policy advice for organizations and regulators, namely audits of model classes instead of single models, a version record for every model response, and re-audits triggered by model changes.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Augmenting Pretrained Language Models with N-gram Embeddings through Incremental Training
items.abstract: As a new scaling technique for large language models, the n-gram embedding improves the base ability of a model while adding almost no inference cost. Mainstream research realizes it through joint training of the n-gram embedding with the backbone, which severely restricts the settings in which an n-gram embedding can be used. We therefore propose training an n-gram embedding onto an existing model through incremental training, to extend where the technique can deliver value. Specifically, we explore several settings of the n-gram embedding under incremental training---the learning rate of the embedding, the vocabulary size, and the injection position---and train an n-gram embedding onto the existing model under the best configuration. Experiments show that the best configuration under incremental training does not fully coincide with that under pretraining; moreover, the incrementally trained knowledge is written predominantly into the n-gram embedding, while the general ability of the backbone is retained throughout this training process.

items.title: Automation, AI and the Changing Skills Demand for University Graduates: A Comparative Qualitative Study across Four Economic Sectors
items.abstract: Abstract Automation, digitalization, and, more recently, generative artificial intelligence (gAI) are changing the skill sets employers demand. However, understanding remains limited about how different sector-level stakeholders in developing countries perceive these innovations, and about these technologies' impact on university graduates' employability. The comparative qualitative study draws on 60 interviews with graduates, employer representatives and academics, five of each type per sector, in four Bangladeshi sectors (readymade garments and textiles (RMG); information and communication technology and IT-enabled services (ICT/ITES); banking and financial services; logistics and supply chain management), as well as multi-sector comparative data. Reflexive thematic analysis yielded cross-sector themes, which include framing of technology and specific discussion of AI in ICT/ITES, disciplinary expertise being necessary but no longer sufficient, with digital, data and adaptive capabilities increasingly essential and learned largely outside formal programmes, cross-sector problems with institutional coordination due to curricula lag (the mode and extent of lag varies according to discipline), reasons why these results should not be taken as an indication of job loss and the impact of gAI, as well as sector-specific and generic implications for universities, sectors and employer associations with clear links to the data. Shortcomings include reliance on perceptions, small cell sizes across multiple parameters, and a lack of a worker perspective.

items.title: Awareness, Perceptions, and Practices of Surgical Smoke Management: A Cross-Sectional Study Guided by Behavioral Reasoning Theory
items.abstract: Abstract Background Surgical smoke is an occupational health concern for operating theatre personnel because of repeated exposure to potentially hazardous substances. Despite available safety guidance, adherence to surgical smoke management practices remains inconsistent, and the behavioural factors influencing these practices are not well understood. This study aims to examine knowledge, awareness, perceptions, and practices from a behavioural perspective related to surgical smoke safety management among surgeons, anesthetists, and perioperative nurses in an acute hospital in Singapore. Methods A descriptive cross-sectional study was conducted among surgeons, anesthetists, and perioperative nurses who were recruited through convenience sampling. Participants voluntarily completed a validated online questionnaire guided by Westaby’s Behavioral Reasoning Theory. The questionnaire assessed demographics, awareness, perceptions and practices, and surgical smoke-related feedback. Results Among 80 participants, the mean general knowledge score was 1.91 ± 0.76. Most participants demonstrated moderate awareness (80.00%) and moderate perception and practice scores (77.50%). Awareness differed significantly by professional role (p < 0.001), with a significant interaction between professional role and general knowledge (p = 0.030). Nurses had significantly higher perception and practice scores than anesthetists and surgeons (p < 0.001). No significant association was found between awareness and perception and practice scores (p = 0.056). Conclusion The findings indicate persistent gaps in SS knowledge and inconsistent implementation of protective measures. A multifactorial approach combining standardized interdisciplinary education, practical training, engineering controls, and organizational policies is warranted to strengthen SS safety and protect surgical teams and patients from potential exposure.

items.title: Bajillion: Cryptographic Clearing for Micropayments
items.abstract: Much of the web is funded by advertising, a model that erodes as humans delegate browsing to AI agents acting on their behalf. A natural replacement is for agents to pay for what they consume, often a fraction of a cent per request. At the scale of web traffic, this could mean tens or even hundreds of millions of payments per second. We present Bajillion, a clearing protocol for scalable micropayments. A sender signs a payment request, and an untrusted operator answers with a preconfirmation, which promises the receiver that it will be paid. Periodically, the operator closes an epoch by posting only the net effect of its payments on chain. Bajillion guarantees that a malicious operator can only omit payments -- it can never debit a sender beyond what it signed, nor misdirect a transfer. Posted balances are therefore finalized immediately and can be withdrawn. By design, senders never have to raise disputes, making it suitable for ephemeral AI agents. A receiver that is shortchanged can prove that a close omitted a preconfirmed payment, which halts the protocol and lets every user exit with its finalized balance. Requests from different senders can be processed independently, allowing the operator to parallelize up to the number of senders. We capture these guarantees in an ideal functionality for accountable clearing and prove that Bajillion realizes it.

items.title: Benefits and Barriers to Human-AI Teaming for Crisis Counseling
items.abstract: Background: AI systems are increasingly deployed to support mental health clinicians, yet real-world evidence remains limited. In crisis counseling, where clients often seek human connection, understanding whether AI augmentation preserves or undermines meaningful human engagement is essential. Methods: In a mixed-methods study of a counselor-facing AI copilot on a WhatsApp-based crisis hotline in India (Mar.-Oct. 2025), counselors could request, edit, and send AI messages. We analyzed 20 interviews, 8 shadowing sessions, 56 survey responses, and edits in 27,778 copilot messages from 108 counselors via thematic analysis (Technology Acceptance Model 2, plus inductive coding of emergent factors), and survey statistics. Results: Counselors reported high copilot acceptance (survey): 98.2% found it helpful; 89.3% likely to continue use; 80.4% reported efficiency gains. Interviews highlighted sentence scaffolding, empathetic phrasing, stress reduction, catching missed details, and efficiency. Barriers (survey) included repetitive outputs (23.2%), lack of context (17.9%), and authenticity concerns (10.7%). While 69.6% (survey) reported skill enhancement, interviews surfaced skill atrophy concerns. Counselors frequently accepted copilot suggestions, editing to remove questions, adjust tone, or personalize style. Conclusion: In one of the largest real-world deployments of a counselor-facing mental health AI copilot, counselors reported reduced cognitive load, empathetic communication, and greater efficiency, alongside concerns about skill atrophy, authenticity, and over-reliance. In settings like crisis counseling where clients seek human connection, AI tools must balance operational support with preserving clinical skill and genuine therapeutic engagement. Designs soliciting approval or editing of complete drafts may overweight efficiency at the expense of sustained human engagement.

items.title: Better Questions or Better Questioning? Student-AI Co-Creation and Higher-Order Thinking in Transdisciplinary Engineering and Design Education
items.abstract: As higher education increasingly adopts transdisciplinary frameworks to address complex societal challenges, cultivating students’ higher-order thinking (HOT) skills has become a key educational goal. These cognitive processes are essential in Human Factors Engineering (HFE), which requires students to address wicked problems inherent in transdisciplinary human-technology systems. However, traditional HFE curricula often emphasise rote memorisation of scientific theories. Meanwhile, the widespread adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) has altered how students engage with academic content by enabling instant access to AI-generated responses. Despite increasing interest in AI-assisted learning, empirical evidence examining LLMs as co-creative partners in activities designed to support HOT remains limited. This quasi-experimental study compares two cohorts in an undergraduate HFE course, in which students either generated exam questions independently or co-created questions with an LLM. A total of 166 multiple-choice questions were collected and classified according to Bloom’s Taxonomy by two independent raters. Results indicate that the LLM-collaboration group produced a significantly higher proportion of higher-order questions. Among student-level factors, the number of student-AI dialogue turns was associated with question cognitive level, whereas self-reported AI usage frequency, metacognitive awareness and prior AI experience were not. Additionally, whether students adopted the AI’s suggested question or wrote their own after the dialogue did not affect question cognitive level. An exploratory analysis suggested that the number of turns in which students critically engaged with AI outputs was marginally associated with higher question cognitive level. These findings highlight the potential value of student-AI dialogue logs as a complementary source of assessment evidence.

items.title: Beyond Bilingual: Studying Quadrilingual Code-Switching with Conversational AI
items.abstract: Multilingual speakers choose languages by topic and conversation partner. Large language models (LLMs) support these languages unequally. Research on code-switching with conversational AI has mostly examined bilingual pairs of well-resourced languages. In Curaçao and Aruba, many people use Dutch, English, Spanish, and the low-resource Creole Papiamentu/o. In a preregistered study, 42 university students held two five-minute chatbot conversations, one about university life and one about local food and culture. Surveys assessed language background, AI use, and switching comfort. 20 international students in Curaçao formed a comparison sample. Participants switched between turns and rarely mixed languages within a message. English dominated both conversations. Participants switched more often in the cultural conversation, where Papiamentu/o and Spanish rose from 15% to 24% of messages. Self-reports showed no lower comfort switching with the chatbot than with a person. Conversational agents must follow turn-by-turn language changes and handle local low-resource languages well.

items.title: Beyond legal compliance: unpacking the “dream candidate” construct and its impact on diversity in hiring from HR professionals' perspective
items.abstract: Purpose In this paper, we explore the cultural production of the “dream candidate” from the perspective of HR workers, to elicit potential for future diversity and inclusion work. Design/methodology/approach We carried out semi-structured interviews with 17 HR officers in Norway, essential mediators between employers and candidates. We asked informants to define the “dream candidate” and analyzed how they made sense of the concept, and relatedly, how they constructed their expertise and role and navigated expectations, concerns and ideals in the hiring process. Findings Instead of listing ideal traits, our informants critiqued the dream candidate concept, framing it as a set of unreasonably ambitious requirements imposed by managers, including qualifications, experience and “culture fit”. While informants constructed their own role as the legal experts in the hiring process, they never mentioned the identity categories central to the law and to most theories of how inequality operates in organizations (such as gender or race). Rather, they critically highlighted managers' tendency to prioritize candidates who resemble either themselves or current employees and acknowledged that they also shared this tendency. Originality/value The study explores the “dream candidate” construct as a culturally produced and contested concept. The analysis shows that HR professionals navigate organizational desires for “sameness” (homosocial reproduction) by silencing societal demands for diversity (legal framework). It shows how HR professionals in a Scandinavian context describe their role in hiring and in producing inequality, and highlights the limits of focusing solely on legally protected identity categories to understand and address it.

items.title: Bookkeeping Is Not Judgement: EJBench, an Engineering Judgement Benchmark Built from a Conjugate Heat Transfer Design Campaign
items.abstract: We introduce EJBench, a benchmark of engineering judgement: whether a model can predict how a design behaves at new conditions from a few earlier results, and decide on it. Unlike engineering benchmarks that test whether an agent can operate simulation or CAD software, EJBench is software-agnostic and asks what an engineer would conclude without running a simulation. Its tasks come from a conjugate heat transfer design campaign for battery cold plates, in three families: matching unlabelled test results to their operating points, choosing which stored runs to reveal before signing off a design, and ranking new duties by peak cell temperature. Every answer is taken from a converged simulation, not from an LLM judge. The best of ten frontier models, GPT-6 Astra, scores 0.71, and models state almost the same confidence on tasks they get wrong as on tasks they get right. We also post-train Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA and reinforcement learning, rewarded by the share of answer criteria the simulation results confirm; on the held-out test split its score rises from 0.071 to 0.106. We release the train, validation and test splits, the evaluation harness and the leaderboard.

items.title: Bridge-RoadLM: Building a Domain-Adapted Large Language Model for Bridge Pavement Maintenance Based on Authoritative Specification Corpora and Efficient Parameter Fine-Tuning
items.abstract: Abstract General large language models (LLMs) often have limited reliability when addressing specialized bridge pavement maintenance tasks. This study proposes Bridge-RoadLM, a domain-adapted framework for preliminary bridge pavement maintenance support. We developed an automated data engineering pipeline to construct the Bridge-Road Corpus, comprising 10,000 instruction-following samples derived from authoritative specifications and technical documents. Using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT/LoRA), representative Qwen, DeepSeek, LLaMA, and Gemma models were adapted to bridge pavement maintenance tasks. A multilevel evaluation framework was established, including automated linguistic metrics, a 500-question expert-validated test bank, and a blinded multiengineer evaluation of open-ended inspection-report-style cases. Results show improved controlled task performance for several fine-tuned models, and the strongest improvement was for Qwen3-8B. Its accuracy in pavement defect diagnosis increased from 45.0% to 81.0%, with 95% Wilson confidence intervals of 35.6%–54.8% and 72.2%–87.5%, respectively. Its accuracy in bridge monitoring and maintenance increased from 25.0% to 75.0%, with 95% Wilson confidence intervals of 17.5%–34.3% and 65.7%–82.5%, respectively. In the blinded open-ended evaluation, six engineers with 10–17 years of professional experience scored anonymized model outputs using five predefined criteria: correctness, completeness, traceability, hallucination control, and safety. Qwen3-8B achieved the highest average score among the nine evaluated models. The results also show that fine-tuning effects varied across model families, indicating that domain-specific PEFT does not uniformly improve all LLMs. Overall, this study provides a specification-based instruction corpus and a controlled evaluation workflow for adapting locally deployable LLMs to bridge pavement maintenance, supporting preliminary specification referencing, defect interpretation, and draft-level maintenance-plan preparation within a human-in-the-loop workflow.
